item.title: APEC-year momentum fuels robust CIIE presence as Asia-Pacific economies tap China's open market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 08:24:00
People visit the booth of Honda, a nine-year attendee of the China International Import Expo (CIIE), at the exhibition area of Automobile and Smart Mobility during the ninth CIIE in east China's Shanghai, Nov. 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Lingyi) As China hosts the 2026 APEC year, the ongoing ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) serves as a tangible demonstration of the Asia-Pacific pursuit of open regionalism, bringing together established multinationals, rising SMEs and industry innovators to turn China's enormous market potential into shared opportunities for the whole region. Running from Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports has drawn wide-ranging delegations and exhibitors from across the Asia-Pacific. Southeast Asian players, including Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore, alongside economies in Oceania and Northeast Asia, have brought consumer goods, advanced technologies and innovative services to the exhibition halls. Paijit Viboontanasarn, vice chairman and secretary general of the Thai Chamber of Commerce in China, said in an interview with Xinhua that the CIIE offers Thai businesses a gateway to the Chinese market, helping smaller firms find customers and test business models while enabling larger companies to deepen cooperation. "Beyond securing orders, the CIIE allows businesses to test whether their products and business models appeal to Chinese consumers," Paijit said. He described the expo in three words: "unique," "opportunity," and "openness," citing its import focus, opportunities for businesses of all sizes, and participation from across the world. A staff member serves macadamia oil from Australia at the exhibition area of Food and Agricultural Products during the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, east China, Nov. 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu) Thai brands are putting this into practice. Botanical fragrance maker Phutawan and snack producer MagMag are showcasing their signature products at this year's expo. "Trade goes both ways," said Nonthakogh Panyapadhm, founder and CEO of MagMag. "Business can last only if both sides benefit." Mark Lee, chairman of the Singapore Business Federation, noted that for Singapore businesses, the value of attending the CIIE "deepens over time." "Many of our companies begin by using the CIIE to build visibility and gather market insights. Over several years, those initial engagements can grow into distribution agreements, joint ventures, and in some cases, regional partnerships that extend beyond China into Southeast Asia," Lee told Xinhua. The federation is leading a 54-company Singapore delegation for the ninth consecutive edition of the expo. Samsung, the South Korean conglomerate, marks its ninth straight year at the CIIE. Zhang Daijun, senior vice president of Samsung China, pointed out that the group keeps expanding its high-end investment and local R&D footprint in China. "China's firm commitment to expanding high-standard opening up has created more opportunities for international enterprises, and provided a stable and predictable environment for their development, injecting greater certainty into global trade cooperation," Zhang said. People communicate at the exhibition area of Food and Agricultural Products during the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, east China, Nov. 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Haoming) From the Southern Hemisphere, Australian and New Zealand enterprises are also actively engaging with Chinese consumers via the expo. Rhys Roberts, national president and chair of the Australia China Business Council, said what matters most to Australian members is what happens after the expo. "Conversations that start on the show floor become distribution agreements, repeat orders and long-term partnerships, and that is where the real value lies," he said. Sanchia Yonge, chief executive of New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, regards the CIIE as a valuable opportunity for New Zealand exporters to showcase products, understand the evolving Chinese market, strengthen brand awareness, and connect with customers and partners for long-term growth. Blis Technologies, a New Zealand biotechnology company, is experiencing a new milestone this year, as it will have its own independent booth at the Shanghai expo. In just two years, sales of its oral probiotics products in China have exceeded 100,000 orders. It's very important to attend the expo on a regular basis because the Chinese market is changing quickly, said Scott Johnson, CEO of Blis Technologies. Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia, commented that the CIIE serves as a vital "gateway" for regional small and medium-sized enterprises to tap the Chinese market and build resilient trade networks amid shifting global dynamics. "China gives opportunities to countries all across the globe," he said. "We need an open system where people with small and medium-sized enterprises, whether in Africa, Indonesia, Vanuatu, or Fiji, have the opportunity to trade across the globe based on WTO rules."

item.title: 'US data, computing in China' is more than just a tongue-in-cheek phrase: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 23:05:00
AI Photo: VCG In the era of AI, the US is tested not only on its innovative capacity but also on its ability to coordinate public interests and objectively recognize the strengths of other countries. The simple insight from "US data, computing in China" lies in the need for open perspectives and pragmatic cooperation in development. Could North American tech companies choose to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in China? Following the conclusion of the US midterm elections, the debate surrounding AI data centers has moved further onto the US public policy agenda. Against this backdrop, a tongue-in-cheek phrase - "US data, computing in China" - has suddenly gained traction online. The idea behind it is that if the construction of data centers in the US faces obstacles, American tech companies may have little choice but to build more offshore data centers. China is one of the few economies in the world with the equipment supply chains and power infrastructure needed to support such facilities. In theory, "US data, computing in China" could therefore represent a solution for the optimal allocation of resources. The emergence of this online quip reflects a real problem: the bottlenecks facing the expansion of AI computing capacity in the US. As a global AI powerhouse, the US is experiencing a surge in demand for computing power, yet upgrades to its power grid infrastructure are lagging significantly behind. Large-scale computing clusters face lengthy waits for grid connection approvals. In addition, following the midterm elections, a growing number of measures restricting data center development may be passed, casting considerable uncertainty over whether new data center projects can move forward. Meanwhile, data centers in the US are expensive and time-consuming to build. Despite continued capital investment, computing capacity is being delivered at a sluggish pace, failing to keep up with the rapid evolution of AI models and customer demand. The gap between supply and demand continues to widen. China, by contrast, offers lower energy costs, more stable power supplies and a more comprehensive supporting industrial ecosystem. More importantly, China has the capacity to coordinate industrial development with infrastructure construction. Initiatives such as the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of a nationwide integrated computing network emphasize regional coordination, the integration of computing power and electricity, and security safeguards. Together, they provide an institutional framework and safeguard for matching computing demand with available resources. China's ability to execute large-scale engineering projects, its supporting infrastructure and its capacity for long-term planning all have the potential to reduce construction coordination costs. Some estimates suggest that data center projects in the US generally take more than three years to complete, while comparable 100-megawatt projects in China can now be delivered in about 12 months. Construction costs per megawatt are estimated to be around $8 million to $12 million in the US, compared with approximately $5.5 million to $6.5 million in China. In this sense, "US data, computing in China" could be a viable avenue for cooperation. The US has accumulated considerable strengths in frontier research and software ecosystems, while China excels in various aspects, including industrial supply chains, engineering and construction capabilities, the number of engineers, and the availability of diverse application scenarios. If the two countries can leverage these complementary strengths in appropriate areas, they could help reduce the overall costs of AI development, ease resource constraints and extend the benefits of technological progress to a broader segment of society. Comparative advantages can be jointly created and continuously enhanced through cooperation. Of course, such cooperation would require clearly defined boundaries. Data involving national security, personal privacy and critical infrastructure should be subject to strict safeguards. Cross-border computing services would also need to take into account network latency, data transmission costs, intellectual property rights and regulatory compliance requirements, among other factors. However, why does this seemingly reasonable solution become a subject of ridicule in reality? The reason is obvious: Washington's political thinking of abusing the concept of security in relation to technology issues. For some time now, the US has weaponized digital elements such as computing power, chips, and data to a high degree. The export control list keeps getting longer, restrictions on advanced chips to China are tightening layer by layer, and investment review mechanisms are increasingly fortified. Not to mention, relocating the US computing power center to China, even specific projects that US and Chinese companies currently want to collaborate on, could easily be thrust under the political microscope and subjected to intense scrutiny amid the increasingly toxic political climate in the US. From a certain perspective, "US data, computing in China" is less about offering advice to American companies and more about netizens mocking Washington's "decoupling and disruption of industrial and supply chains" in the field of digital technology. Although "US data, computing in China" is far from reality, further extending the cooperation list in the AI field between China and the US is possible and necessary. The Chinese people's aspiration for a better life and the American people's desire to improve their lives and revitalize industries share a space of mutual interest. If "Make America Great Again" includes lowering living costs, increasing quality employment, and improving public facilities, then engaging in pragmatic cooperation with China can also be a viable option for achieving these goals. Mutual success should reflect tangible benefits that both peoples can perceive. At the same time, as two influential entities in the global AI field, it is also the shared responsibility of both countries to improve AI global governance and promote inclusive development. In the era of AI, the US is tested not only on its innovative capacity but also on its ability to coordinate public interests and objectively recognize the strengths of other countries. The simple insight from "US data, computing in China" lies in the need for open perspectives and pragmatic cooperation in development. As long as the US can shed its Cold War mentality and move toward China, adhering to a people-centered approach and developing AI for the positive and for good, there will still be opportunities to transform real pressures into momentum for common development, allowing AI to truly serve the progress of humanity. The world needs such cooperation.

item.title: GT Voice: China's cruise takeoff will create wider room for co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 21:54:00
Photo: VCG China's two domestically built large cruise ships were spotted berthing side by side at Wusongkou in Shanghai on Sunday, in what was reportedly their first such encounter. Adora Magic City , the country's first homegrown large cruise ship, was joined by the newly delivered Adora Flora City . Large cruise ships are among the most complex engineering undertakings in the global industrial system. The sight of the two vessels side by side in Shanghai captures a turning point for China's shipbuilding industry, from the breakthrough of building the first large cruise ship to the capacity for serial production. But for the international shipbuilding industry, there is more to this story. The gathering at Wusongkou is only the beginning. Adora Flora City will begin its inaugural season on November 22. The ship is entering a market with growing consumer demand. China has become one of the fastest-growing cruise markets in Asia and in the world. According to an industry report, the country handled 1.265 million cruise passenger trips in the first 11 months of 2025, up 27.8 percent year-on-year. China's advances in large cruise shipbuilding are set to intensify competition in the global shipbuilding industry. As Chinese shipyards continue to develop their technological capabilities, that competition is likely to become more pronounced. But that is only one side of the story. China's expanding cruise market is creating new commercial opportunities for international companies, even as Chinese shipbuilders become more competitive. China's progress in the industry is not only changing the competitive landscape but also expanding the market for the industry as a whole. Shipbuilding is an extraordinarily complex industry, underpinned by an extensive network of suppliers and supporting businesses. Large cruise ships take that complexity to another level. Adora Flora City , for instance, reportedly incorporates more than 25 million components, drawing on a network of 1,500 suppliers from China and abroad. These figures offer a glimpse of the commercial ecosystem surrounding China's shipbuilding industry, linking shipyards with suppliers and businesses across the wider value chain in an intricate web of commercial relationships. Two developments are advancing China's shipbuilding industry: technological progress and the expanding consumer market. Both need to be seen in the context of the industry's extensive supply chain. As China's shipbuilding sector moves forward, so does the wider industrial ecosystem around it which will generate greater opportunities for Chinese and international companies alike. The scale of the Chinese market offers international companies more than one way to participate in its growth. They can compete with Chinese shipbuilders, while also finding opportunities to cooperate by supplying technologies, specialized equipment and services. As the industry develops, the growing industrial network is creating more commercial opportunities that extend well beyond shipyards. South Korea has maintained a strong position in high-value and high-tech shipbuilding, while Japan and some European countries retain strengths in specialized segments, including cruise ship construction. Such differences reflect the depth of expertise across the global shipbuilding industry. China's rapid progress has led some international observers to focus on the competitive pressure the global industry faces. But that perspective risks obscuring a parallel development: the scope for cooperation across the industry's supply chain is expanding alongside China's own capabilities. The more Chinese shipbuilding industry grows, the greater the potential for international companies to participate in that growth. That opportunity, however, will not be there for the taking. International suppliers will need to offer specialized equipment and advanced services that meet the increasingly sophisticated demands of Chinese shipbuilders and customers. The two luxury cruisers together at Wusongkou offer a snapshot of China's rapid manufacturing progress. For international companies, this signals a wider field of cooperation and opportunities. To bag these opportunities will require a competitive edge in technology and expertise.

item.title: CPC launches election of 2,360 delegates for 21st national congress, emphasizing political standards, grassroots representation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 20:44:00
File photo: VCG The Communist Party of China (CPC) has launched the process of electing 2,360 delegates to its 21st National Congress, scheduled to convene in Beijing in the second half of 2027, with the arrangements placing political standards at the forefront while emphasizing grassroots participation, strict electoral discipline and representation of workers in new forms of employment. An official from the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee underscored on Sunday the significance of the delegate election, describing it as crucial for the successful convening of the 21st CPC National Congress, a practical step in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance and strengthening intra-Party political life, and a means of mobilizing Party members to fulfill the CPC's missions and tasks. The CPC Central Committee has issued a circular making comprehensive arrangements for the election, while the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee has outlined detailed requirements for its implementation, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. According to the report, 2,360 delegates, 60 more than at the previous Party congress, will be elected by 38 electoral units across the country. The election process is scheduled to conclude by the end of June 2027. According to an official from the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee, the allocation of delegate seats takes into account changes in the size of the Party's membership and organizational structure, as well as the number of Party organizations and arrangements at previous congresses. Su Wei, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Chongqing Municipal Committee, told the Global Times on Sunday that the increase of 60 delegate seats reflects the continued growth of the CPC's membership and grassroots organizational network. Zhang Xixian, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, told the Global Times on Sunday the composition of delegates should also reflect changes in China's economic and social development, including the rise of new employment groups, advances in scientific and technological innovation, industrial upgrading and evolving demands in social governance. According to an explainer article published by Xinhua on Sunday, the 21st CPC National Congress will be "a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country," as a new CPC Central Committee and a new CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection will be elected. The 2,360 delegates to be elected should be outstanding Party members who carry the trust of more than 101 million CPC members and over 5.4 million Party organizations as they fulfill their duties at the congress. An organization department official said in an interview with Xinhua which was published on Sunday that the congress will review the work of the previous five years, determine the Party's future direction, development objectives and action plans, and elect new central leadership bodies. During the congress, delegates will review reports, reflect the opinions and demands of Party members and the public, deliberate on major issues and participate in elections. The official also emphasized that the qualifications, capabilities and conduct of delegates directly affect the quality of deliberations and decision-making at the congress, highlighting the importance of rigorous selection procedures. Political standards first Political standards have been placed at the forefront of the selection process, alongside strict eligibility criteria, rigorous electoral procedures, and strict enforcement of electoral discipline, to ensure that those elected are of high caliber, broadly representative and supported by Party members, and that the delegation has a balanced composition, according to Xinhua. The organization department official further explained in the interview that political standards are the primary requirement for Party congress delegates, with particular emphasis on political commitment and loyalty to the Party. Candidates who fail to meet political standards will be subject to a one-vote veto. The election arrangements also require rigorous integrity checks and assessments of candidates' moral character and conduct to prevent individuals with unresolved disciplinary or integrity problems from being nominated or elected. The emphasis on political qualifications and integrity checks is closely connected to the CPC's broader efforts to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance, Su said. He noted that political commitment and the implementation of the Party's policies are fundamental requirements for delegates, while strict integrity standards are equally important. Delegates should not only meet political requirements but also serve as examples of integrity and self-discipline, he added. Grassroots representation According to Xinhua, delegates should come from a wide range of fields, including the economy, science and technology, national defense, law enforcement and the justice system, education, public communication, culture, health, sports and social administration. They should also include workers in new forms of employment. Among delegates from provincial-level regions, central financial institutions and central state-owned enterprises in Beijing, Party members working on the front line should generally account for at least one-third. Among delegates from central Party and state departments, the proportion should generally be no less than 15 percent. Particular attention should be paid to recommending model workers, farmers and professionals as candidates. Women Party members and Party members from ethnic minority groups should each make up a certain proportion of the delegates. According to Xinhua, in regions where the new economy and new forms of business are thriving and large numbers of workers are employed in new forms of employment, outstanding Party members from among these workers should also be recommended as candidates. Zhang said the emergence of new employment groups and economic organizations reflects broader changes in China's economic development, making it necessary for grassroots Party organizations to extend their organizational presence and activities into emerging sectors. As new industries and forms of employment expand, Party building should keep pace with economic development, he said, emphasizing that grassroots organizations should not only strengthen organizational coverage but also engage with workers, respond to their concerns and safeguard their legitimate rights and interests. Five-stage election process According to Xinhua's Sunday explainer, the process consists of nomination of candidates, assessment of nominees by electoral units, formation of a preliminary list of candidates, formation of a preparatory list of candidates, and formal election. The Organization Department official said the selection will follow a bottom-up approach that combines recommendations from lower-level organizations with consultations and assessments at higher levels, involving repeated deliberations and selection at successive organizational levels. Grassroots Party organizations and members will be encouraged to participate extensively in recommending and nominating candidates. Selection at successive levels should take into account the opinions of the majority of relevant Party organizations and members. The official also emphasized strict organizational assessments, including competitive assessments and advance announcements of assessments, while requiring electoral units to solicit opinions from grassroots Party organizations, Party congress delegates, Party members and members of the public. The delegates will be elected through a competitive process in which the number of candidates must exceed the number of seats by more than 15 percent, per Xinhua. According to the official arrangements, electoral units may conduct a preliminary election with more candidates than seats before holding a final election with an equal number of candidates and seats, or proceed directly to a competitive final election. Those elected will undergo an additional qualification review before the national congress convenes. The Organization Department official described the election as an important channel through which Party members exercise their democratic rights and participate in internal Party political life in accordance with the principle of democratic centralism. Strict discipline Electoral discipline constitutes another major component of the arrangements, with the CPC Central Committee calling for strengthened supervision throughout the process and zero tolerance for violations of rules, discipline and laws. According to Xinhua, political, organizational and electoral disciplines must be strictly observed, with efforts made to prevent vote-buying and other electoral violations and strengthen oversight and enforcement. The CPC Central Committee has also explicitly called for drawing lessons from previous cases involving vote-buying and disruption of elections in Hengyang, Central China's Hunan Province, Nanchong, Southwest China's Sichuan Province, and Northeast China's Liaoning Province. The Organization Department official stressed that oversight, investigation and accountability should be strengthened, with violations of electoral discipline subject to strict investigation and punishment. The arrangements also require the election process to serve as an opportunity for education on Party theory, conduct, discipline and history, while encouraging Party members and officials to fulfill their responsibilities. Looking ahead, Su noted that the 21st CPC National Congress will convene at a crucial stage in China's efforts to realize socialist modernization by 2035. He said that delegates elected to the upcoming congress, particularly those who may serve consecutive terms, could play an important role during a period closely aligned with the country's 2035 development objectives. Selecting qualified delegates is therefore significant not only for the successful convening of the congress but also for advancing the Party's longer-term development agenda. Du Qiongfang also contributed to the story.

item.title: China's Xiamen joins the bid to host High Seas Treaty secretariat: Why this race matters to the Global North and South
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 20:42:00
Chinese white dolphins, a national first-class protected wild animal species, appear on the sea surface, swimming and chasing the waves in Qinzhou, South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on January 9, 2026. Photo: VCG Beside the Mazu Cultural Square in Xiamen, East China's Fujian Province, a modern high-rise building surrounded by greenery and overlooking the sea has been prepared for a special purpose: to serve as the headquarters of the secretariat of the UN treaty on marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), also known as the High Seas Treaty. On January 17, the landmark treaty entered into force after nearly two decades of negotiations, marking a new chapter in global ocean governance. As its first Conference of the Parties (COP) approaches, competition to host the secretariat is heating up, with Xiamen, Brussels in Belgium and Valparaiso in Chile vying for the role. Why has a treaty on marine biodiversity attracted such international attention? And why are three countries competing to host its permanent secretariat? Against the backdrop of growing tensions over high-seas ecological conservation and resource development worldwide, the future implementation of this international system and its implications for global governance have drawn widespread attention. The urban coastline in Xiamen, East China's Fujian Province Photo: VCG New rules for the high seas The high seas, covering roughly 60 percent of the world's oceans, contain vast marine resources shared by humanity. Yet significant gaps have long existed in the governance of areas beyond national jurisdiction. A report titled "The BBNJ Agreement: Status, Functions, Prospects and China's Role" released on November 5 by the China Institute for Marine Affairs under China's Ministry of Natural Resources, argues that the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) alone is no longer sufficient to address emerging challenges. Take the much-discussed seabed mineral mining in recent years as an example. In January, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration revised procedures under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act to streamline permit applications. A US subsidiary of a Canadian metals company subsequently applied for combined exploration and commercial recovery rights covering approximately 65,000 square kilometers of international seabed between Hawaii and Mexico. Meanwhile, US authorities advanced seabed mining-related activities near American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands. This move carries a tangible risk of issuing commercial mining permits by bypassing the multilateral framework of the International Seabed Authority under the United Nations. It has drawn criticism from deep-sea conservation coalitions, multiple developing countries and some developed nations, which argue that it violates the principle of the "common heritage of mankind," seeks to privatize resources in the international seabed area, and undermines the multilateral governance order. "Deep-sea microorganisms may become sources of new medicines and materials. But how should the benefits of scientific discoveries be shared? Who should protect ecologically important areas on the high seas? And who should assess and prevent environmental damage?" Zheng Miaozhuang, a researcher at the China Institute for Marine Affairs and contributor to the aforementioned report "The BBNJ Agreement: Status, Functions, Prospects and China's Role," told the Global Times. Although UNCLOS established fundamental principles, including freedom of the high seas and the common heritage of humankind, rapid technological advances and expanding ocean activities have created new governance challenges, Zheng explained. The BBNJ Agreement seeks to fill these gaps through four pillars: marine genetic resources and benefit-sharing; area-based management tools, including marine protected areas; environmental impact assessments; and capacity-building and marine technology transfer. "This is a genuine institutional breakthrough," Zheng said. The Agreement establishes, for the first time, a benefit-sharing arrangement for deep-sea genetic resources and their "genetic data," provides a legal basis for establishing protected areas on the high seas and in the international seabed area for the first time, and also refines environmental assessment, capacity-building and technology transfer. But reaching the agreement was far from easy. Negotiations were repeatedly challenged by differences over benefit-sharing, marine protected areas and the transparency of environmental impact assessments. Nevertheless, countries eventually reached compromises to address challenges that transcend national boundaries. Developing countries were particularly concerned about fairness, Zheng noted. They wanted to ensure that deep-sea research and resource development would not be dominated by a handful of technologically advanced nations, while most countries, including China, supported stronger protection of vulnerable marine ecosystems. "Who can explore the deep sea, use its resources and share the benefits is not just a technological question, but one of fairness in global governance," Xu Heyun, deputy director of the China Institute for Marine Affairs under China's Ministry of Natural Resources, told the Global Times. She said the BBNJ Agreement promotes equitable participation through information sharing, scientific cooperation, financial support and technology transfer, helping bridge differences among countries. China played an active role throughout the negotiations, according to the report, working to bridge North-South differences, promote equitable benefit sharing from marine genetic resources, strengthen marine biodiversity protection and improve the transparency of environmental impact assessments. "China advocated a package solution to the four major issues, balancing conservation with sustainable use. Marine protected areas must not become 'paper parks,' while developing countries need not just assistance, but the capacity to develop independently," Xu said. China signed the treaty on September 20, 2023, its opening day for signature, and deposited its instrument of ratification on December 15, 2025, demonstrating its commitment to implementation. The proposed office premises for the BBNJ secretariat in Xiamen, China. Photo: Fan Wei/Global Times Why is China bidding to host the secretariat? Turning the treaty into an operational system requires permanent institutions. Under the BBNJ Agreement, the COP serves as the highest decision-making body, while the secretariat provides administrative, logistical and meeting support and manages the clearing-house mechanism for information exchange. As implementation advances, the secretariat will also support cooperation on marine genetic resources, marine protected areas, environmental assessments and capacity-building for developing countries. "The secretariat is not a 'world government' governing the high seas," Zhao Chang, a researcher at the China Institute for Marine Affairs, told the Global Times. "It has no independent enforcement authority and cannot make decisions on behalf of the parties. Rather, it is an essential institution connecting governments, research organizations and international bodies." According to previously announced arrangements, the first COP is scheduled for January 11-22, 2027, at the UN Headquarters in New York, with the location of the secretariat among the major decisions to be made. Xiamen, Brussels and Valparaiso each bring different advantages to the competition. For China, the bid is primarily about assuming long-term responsibilities as a host country and supporting more inclusive ocean governance. Major international marine institutions have traditionally been concentrated in Europe. Hosting the secretariat in Asia, home to numerous maritime nations and a rapidly growing blue economy, could improve geographical representation and make participation more accessible to developing countries, according to Zheng. Zhao stressed that China's bid is not intended to secure special decision-making powers. "Global ocean governance should not be dominated by the voices of a few countries," he said. "We must protect the oceans while respecting countries' legitimate needs for scientific research and development." Xu also placed the bid in a broader historical context. "More than 600 years ago, Zheng He's voyages promoted exchanges and friendship through the oceans. Today, China remains committed to both marine conservation and sustainable use, and hopes to deepen international maritime cooperation through this bid," Xu said. What can China bring to global ocean governance? Hosting an international treaty secretariat requires more than political commitment or suitable office facilities. Zheng noted that these include whether office and meeting venues are well-equipped, whether international transportation and personnel exchanges are convenient, whether legal status and privileges and immunities are guaranteed, whether funding support can be sustained, and whether there is room for long-term development - all of which are important factors for the parties to assess a bid proposal. Zheng said China's strengths lie in its marine research capabilities, conservation experience, international partnerships and capacity to assist developing countries. According to the report "The BBNJ Agreement: Status, Functions, Prospects and China's Role," China has established an integrated ocean research system comprising research vessels, manned deep-sea submersibles and marine observation facilities. Equipment such as the Jiaolong and Fendouzhe submersibles has strengthened China's capacity to explore deep-sea environments and study marine biodiversity. China has also conducted joint marine research with countries including Bangladesh, provided deep-sea research opportunities for partners such as Indonesia and led international scientific initiatives covering digital deep-sea habitats and ocean data sharing. These efforts could provide scientific support for identifying conservation priorities, monitoring biodiversity and developing area-based management tools. In marine conservation, China has established 353 marine protected areas and implemented 194 major marine ecological restoration projects, according to the report. It is also among the few countries to have achieved a net increase in mangrove coverage. China has accumulated experience in environmental impact assessments through marine surveys in the western Pacific and northern Indian Ocean, providing data and technical expertise that could help developing countries meet their treaty obligations. Capacity-building is another priority. China has signed marine cooperation agreements with more than 50 countries and international organizations, invested approximately 200 million yuan ($28 million) in over 100 livelihood-oriented marine cooperation projects, and provided marine scholarships to 345 professionals from 47 countries and regions. Through joint training platforms, including cooperation with the International Seabed Authority, China has also trained more than 6,000 young researchers and officials from developing countries. Xiamen itself offers advantages as a coastal city with established research and international cooperation networks. It hosts Xiamen University, the Third Institute of Oceanography under the Ministry of Natural Resources, and platforms including the APEC Marine Sustainable Development Center and the China-ASEAN Marine Cooperation Center. "More importantly, China has proposed a concrete long-term support package for the secretariat, covering office and conference facilities, legal and administrative arrangements, financial support and capacity-building cooperation," Xu said. The BBNJ Agreement's entry into force marks a beginning rather than an endpoint. According to the report, China is ready to take its bid as an opportunity to deepen exchanges with other countries in marine biodiversity conservation, marine scientific research, capacity-building and marine technology cooperation, and to support science-based and cooperation-driven global ocean governance.

item.title: PrimeBOT's 10,000th personal robot rolls off production line as large-scale manufacturing of consumer embodied AI accelerates
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 20:33:00
Humanoid robots by PrimeBOT Photo: VCG Chinese robotics company PrimeBOT said on Sunday that its 10,000th personal robot has rolled off the production line, a milestone in the company's push toward large-scale mass production of consumer-grade embodied artificial intelligence (AI) products. Analysts said that this marks another step forward in the company's large-scale production, supply chain integration and delivery capabilities, helping personal robots move from early-stage mass-production validation to a new phase of scaled manufacturing and laying the foundation for broader market adoption of consumer embodied AI products. The milestone comes just 14 days after PrimeBOT announced the 5,000th unit had been completed on October 25, meaning the company doubled its cumulative output from 5,000 to 10,000 units in two weeks, according to a statement the company sent to the Global Times on Sunday. According to Liu Dongfang, the president of the Q Business Unit (the division responsible for PrimeBOT's robotics line), the scaling up of production underscores the company's progress in building a more mature industrial system. "Behind these numbers is a systematic verification of our manufacturing process, quality management system and supply chain coordination capabilities," he said. Industry observers said that the move from prototype validation and small-batch trial production to the 10,000-unit level is an inflection point for Chinese-made consumer robotics. A robot is no longer just a laboratory concept, but a product that begins to demonstrate the ability to be manufactured consistently, delivered reliably and integrated into real-world scenarios such as homes, retail services and education. The 10,000-unit milestone is significant not only for PrimeBOT but also for China's broader personal robotics sector, Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Sunday. Wang added that for personal robots, this indicates the technology is beginning to move beyond the lab and into environments such as households, retail and educational settings, where consistent performance and reliable user experience are essential. PrimeBOT began handing over its first Q1 and T1 personal robots on October 1 in seven Chinese cities including Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hangzhou. Both start at 19,999 yuan ($2,995.43), according to domestic media reports. The company's rapid production ramp-up comes amid rising competition in China's humanoid robotics market, where firms are racing to combine AI, mobility and interactive capabilities into products that can function as companions, assistants and service platforms. Hangzhou-based Unitree Robotics has produced about 10,000 to 20,000 G1 humanoid robots since the model's launch in May 2024, the company's founder Wang Xingxing said. He said that he expects commercial services to adopt robots faster than households or industrial users. Chinese humanoid robot producers are widening their lead over global rivals, accounting for more than 97 percent of worldwide shipments in the first half of 2026, according to market research firm Smart Analytics Global (SAG). SAG said that Chinese robotics company AgiBot overtook Unitree Robotics for the first time to become the world's largest humanoid robot supplier by shipments. AgiBot shipped about 8,400 units, capturing 44 percent of the global market, while Unitree delivered about 5,900 units. China has developed more than 400 complete humanoid robot products, accounting for more than half of the world's total, highlighting the country's rapidly expanding presence in the robotics sector, official data showed. In the first half of the year, China-developed quadruped robots accounted for nearly 70 percent of global sales, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology China also expects its production of humanoid robots to surpass 100,000 units this year, as the country accelerates efforts to bring AI from laboratories into factories. "That growth is increasingly propelled by deep integration with generative AI, factory automation and logistics operators," Wang said. Analysts said that strong government support, abundant funding and China's broad manufacturing ecosystem are accelerating this transition, helping robotics vendors move from prototypes toward larger-scale commercial deployment.

item.title: Indian companies actively attend 9th CIIE, eyeing deals in the vast market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 20:31:00
An Indian exhibitor arranges display items at the 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai on November 7, 2026. Photo: Ma Jingjing/Global Times On Saturday morning, the consumer goods section of the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai was already bustling with activity. About a dozen Indian enterprises lined the halls, their booths adorned with vibrant displays of Kashmir cashmere scarves, hand-carved wooden furniture, intricate handicrafts, and aromatic Indian incense. Every now and then, visitors stopped by to inquire about prices, run their fingers across the soft fabrics, or take photos of the exquisite pieces. Amid the lively chatter and occasional bursts of laughter, some Indian exhibitors warmly greeted potential clients in Chinese, showing eagerness to expand their presence in the vast Chinese market amid the improving economic and trade relationship between China and India. Active participation Among them was Shabir Ahmad Ahangar, whose booth was draped in an elegant array of cashmere scarves in rich jewel tones. As he carefully straightened a stack of shawls and hung a particularly fine piece on the rack for better display, he noticed visitors coming and immediately flashed a broad smile. Switching effortlessly between Chinese and English, he told the Global Times that he has come to the CIIE many times. His booth has expanded from about 5 square meters when he first attended the CIIE several years ago to 20 square meters this year. Last year, the company's sales at the expo were pretty good, and the expectation is high this year, he said, adding that the expo is crucial for expanding his customer base, which now spans not only China but also markets like Vietnam and Mongolia. Just a few steps away, at the Sudha India International booth, Suyash Mehta was helping refine a hand-made chair with his father, owner of the Indian company. "This is my first time here, but my father has attended many times," Mehta said. "We attend different expos, not just in Shanghai, but in different cities as well, like in Beijing, Kunming [in Southwest China's Yunnan Province,] and [North China's] Tianjin. We attended every exhibition this year," he said, noting that China, which takes about 30 percent market share for the company, is one of the important markets. Compared with Mehta, Shahzad Ahmad, CEO of Prince Trading Co, was more familiar with the Chinese market as he first came to China in 2014. With his branch and warehouse based in Tianjin, he has deeply integrated into the Chinese business ecosystem. "Everything is on mobile," he joked, referring to how he manages his operations seamlessly with the help of various smart applications in China. "We modify our products according to Chinese culture and Chinese living style," he said. "Our Chinese customers also help us make our products more beautiful. They give us ideas." When the conversation turned to China-India relations, Ahmad's tone grew more reflective yet hopeful. "Business is a good way to make good relations," he said. Improving bilateral ties Chinese experts say the warming business sentiment at the Shanghai expo reflects the deep complementarity between the two economies. Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times on Sunday that the active participation of Indian companies in the CIIE reflects their high expectations for the Chinese market. China possesses a vast consumer market, which holds significant appeal for Indian businesses, Qian said. Indian exhibitors' hopes come amid improving economic and trade relations between China and India. According to data released by China's General Administration of Customs, imports and exports between China and India soared 25.4 percent year-on-year to reach $144.45 billion in the first nine months of 2026. While bilateral trade has reached a new record high, institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, and the list of areas of cooperation has continued to grow. In September, China Southern Airlines flight CZ359 departed from Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport bound for Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi, marking the relaunch of the airline's India services after a six-year suspension. Qian said that China is the world's second-largest economy and one of India's most important trading partners. Improving economic and trade relations with China and expanding bilateral trade and investment cooperation serve India's own economic interests. "India is currently at a critical stage of manufacturing development and industrial restructuring. In this process, India still has strong demand for Chinese supply chains, especially in areas such as electronic components and pharmaceutical raw materials, where the development of Indian manufacturing cannot be separated from products and supply-chain support provided by Chinese companies," Qian said. Reflecting the complementarity of Chinese and Indian industries, the Indian government reportedly approved Indian firm Dixon's joint venture with Chinese smartphone maker Vivo Mobile in July, clearing the way for the companies to set up a smartphone manufacturing company in India. "This is a small step. Much more is needed to fully normalize India-China cooperation in business and the economy in ways that benefit both countries," Sudheendra Kulkarni, an Indian scholar and the founder of India's Forum for a New South Asia, told the Global Times in a recent interview. "India has a large market for consumer and capital goods. China has proven industrial strengths in these areas." Many Indian companies are waiting to form joint ventures with Chinese counterparts across the green energy ecosystem - electric vehicles and batteries, charging infrastructure, recycling and energy storage systems, renewable energy and grid infrastructure, smart meters, transmission systems, and green hydrogen equipment, Kulkarni said.

item.title: Hong Kong's sentencing of Joshua Wong gets Western politicians chirping again
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 19:19:00
In this file photo taken on June 30, 2017, Joshua Wong Chi-fung (front) speaks during an interview in front of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government headquarters in Hong Kong, south China. Photo: Xinhua Ten governments, including the US, Canada, France and Germany, recently issued a joint statement pointing fingers at the case against Joshua Wong Chi-fung, going so far as to call for "an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions." This statement is simply baffling. Who is Wong? He is a Chinese citizen "guilty of conspiracy to collude with a foreign country or external elements to endanger national security." He has repeatedly broken the law, playing an active role in fueling the "black-clad violence" that prevailed in Hong Kong in 2019 and continuing to conspire with external forces to endanger national security and subvert state power. His crimes are serious, the evidence against him is solid and the punishment fits the offenses. He has also admitted to the crimes he committed. Put simply, whoever actively steps forward to stand on the side of this criminal is standing against the spirit of the rule of law. The irony is that these Western political elites, so eager to speak up for Wong, show little leniency toward those involved in violent unrest at home. In the US, following the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, large numbers of rioters who stormed the building and assaulted police officers were sentenced to prison, with the longest sentence reaching 22 years. US media overwhelmingly referred to those involved as "insurrectionists" or "rioters." During the wave of riots that swept across multiple British cities in 2024, then prime minister Keir Starmer explicitly condemned them as "far-right thuggery" and called for swift prosecutions, allowing no room for leniency. The British government and prosecutors also treated incitement on social media as a criminal offense, demanding that platforms cooperate by handing over information and removing inflammatory content. France needs little introduction either: As violent protests continue in the country, French police have been out on the streets using batons to disperse demonstrators. This explains why these politicians only dare to label the case with an abstract term like "unjust prosecution," while saying nothing about how these Hong Kong secessionists incited street violence and directed protesters to storm the Legislative Council and other institutions. They know perfectly well that such acts would constitute unacceptable criminal offenses in any country. Yet, they continue to apply double standards and interfere in Hong Kong affairs, demanding the release of individuals who have endangered national security. Their agenda has nothing to do with the rule of law or human rights. The fact that their joint statement specifically targets Hong Kong's national security law speaks volumes: The law has cut off the political tentacles through which Western forces sought to meddle in Hong Kong and sow chaos. There is a Chinese saying: "If you stopped farming every time you heard a mole cricket chirp, would you ever get any crops planted?" Hong Kong today has long moved beyond the turmoil of the past and is steadily advancing from chaos to stability and from stability to prosperity. Any fantasy of turning Hong Kong into a bridgehead for destabilizing China is doomed to fail. Rather than rushing to plead the case for those who seek to undermine Hong Kong, some Western politicians would do better to put their own houses in order first.

item.title: MSS warns of national security risks, citing lessons from massive data leaks at Japanese firms
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 12:25:00
Photo: VCG Referring to a recent spate of large-scale user data breaches involving Japanese companies, China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) warned on Sunday that massive data leaks, including information related to people's daily lives, could be exploited by foreign spy and intelligence agencies for user profiling and behavioral analysis, threatening national security. According to the MSS, Japan has suffered a spate of large-scale data breaches recently, with more than 115 million records reportedly compromised in the six weeks from September to mid-October. The incidents included the theft of over 22 million customer records from a major software company and the exposure of millions of restaurant membership records. A recent survey found that nearly 30 percent of major Japanese companies said they had experienced actual or suspected data leaks. The MSS warned that the greater the degree of digitalization, the more important it is to remain vigilant against data security risks. A review of a series of data breaches exposed in recent years shows that large-scale data leaks reflect underlying security weaknesses, and that despite varying attack methods, recent incidents have exposed strikingly similar security vulnerabilities. Data breaches threaten national security. In today's complex cyberspace, once massive amounts of data related to people's daily lives and behavioral patterns are leaked, they could be exploited by foreign espionage and intelligence agencies for user profiling, behavioral analysis and targeted infiltration. Such leaks could evolve into more profound cybersecurity threats, endangering national security and social stability, the MSS said. According to the MSS, poor data management is a key vulnerability. Most companies involved in the breaches have long collected user information indiscriminately and retained it beyond necessary periods, resulting in large accumulations of data that become high-risk "data troves." Meanwhile, outdated systems, delayed security patches and lax backend access controls further heighten the risks. Weak employee security awareness is another major vulnerability, with human errors such as sending emails to the wrong recipients, failing to verify information requests and using weak passwords making it easier for attackers to gain access. The MSS cited an example in which an employee of a company, mistakenly believing that an email had come from a business partner and that the matter was urgent, hastily provided sensitive information without first verifying the request by phone. The ministry said such attacks are repeatedly successful precisely because of employees' weak internal security awareness, allowing "human negligence" to become the "biggest vulnerability." Supply chain security is another major vulnerability, with data breaches often stemming from inadequate safeguards and lax management at outsourced service providers and third-party platforms rather than direct attacks on companies' own systems. Supply chain attacks have become a key vector for cyber intrusions, the MSS said. The MSS said data breaches pose multiple risks. First, data breaches threaten individual rights and security, as leaked personal information, including names, addresses, phone numbers and travel records, can be exploited for targeted scams, harassment and identity theft, putting privacy and financial security at risk. Large-scale leaks of business and service data can trigger customer disputes, regulatory penalties and public backlash, undermining public trust and damaging corporate reputations, industry image and service credibility. Therefore, the MSS urged individuals and organizations to strengthen data security by tightening data management, raising security awareness among employees and strictly controlling supply chain risks. Global Times

item.title: China opposes joint statement criticizing HKSAR court's Wong Chi-fung sentencing decision: Chinese embassies in Canada, France and Netherlands
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 10:57:00
In this file photo taken on June 30, 2017, Joshua Wong Chi-fung (front) speaks during an interview in front of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government headquarters in Hong Kong, south China. Photo: Xinhua China strongly opposed a joint statement issued by Canada and several other countries criticizing the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) court's sentencing decision in the Wong Chi-fung case, accusing them of interfering in Hong Kong's judicial affairs and China's internal affairs, said the Chinese embassies in Canada, France and the Netherlands over the weekend. The foreign ministries of Canada, the US, the UK, Australia and other countries issued a joint statement on Friday regarding the sentencing of Wong. In response, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Canada said that Canada had joined certain other countries in issuing the so-called joint statement to criticize the Hong Kong court's sentencing decision in the case, openly interfering in Hong Kong's judicial affairs and China's internal affairs. Hong Kong is a society governed by the rule of law, where compliance with the law and accountability for violations are fundamental principles, the spokesperson said. According to the spokesperson, Wong had long been involved in conspiring with and colluding with foreign or external forces to endanger national security. He continued these activities even after the implementation of the National Security Law. Wong’s actions seriously undermined China's sovereignty and dignity, threatened the vital interests of the Hong Kong people and jeopardized the city's long-term stability and security. Faced with overwhelming facts and evidence, Wong had no grounds to deny his wrongdoing and chose to plead guilty. The Hong Kong court's trial and sentencing decision were lawful and fair, and should not be challenged, the spokesperson said. On Saturday, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in France said that China firmly opposed the joint statement issued on Friday by the foreign ministers of 10 countries and published on the French Foreign Ministry's website, and had lodged solemn representations with the French side. The spokesperson said the statement commented on Wong’s case and interfered in the judicial affairs of the HKSAR. According to the spokesperson, Wong was convicted of "conspiring to collude with foreign country or with external elements to endanger national security" with the evidence against him conclusive and the sentence commensurate with the seriousness of the crime. Wong pleaded guilty to the charges. Hong Kong is a society governed by the rule of law, and relevant cases are handled strictly on the basis of evidence and in accordance with the law. The Chinese central government firmly supports the HKSAR in safeguarding national security and cracking down on acts that endanger national security in accordance with the law, the spokesperson said. The spokesperson urged the French side to act in accordance with the principles of mutual respect and non-interference in each other's internal affairs, genuinely respect China's sovereignty and the rule of law in Hong Kong, and stop making irresponsible remarks about judicial proceedings in the HKSAR. In addition, the Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands also issued a statement on Saturday, voicing firm support for the HKSAR's efforts to punish crimes endangering national security in accordance with the law. According to the embassy, Wong was sentenced by the HKSAR court in accordance with the law for conspiring to collude with a foreign country or with external elements to endanger national security. The Chinese central government firmly supports the HKSAR in safeguarding national security and punishing criminal acts that endanger national security in accordance with the law. Throughout the trial, HKSAR law enforcement, prosecution and judicial authorities handled the case in strict accordance with the law, fully safeguarding the defendant's legal rights. The trial was open, fair and impartial, with rulings based on facts and the law. Hong Kong's judicial authorities exercise their judicial powers independently in accordance with the law, free from any external interference, the embassy said. Hong Kong is part of China, and Hong Kong affairs are purely China's internal affairs the embassy said. It urged the Netherlands and other relevant countries to respect China's sovereignty and the rule of law in the HKSAR, and to stop interfering in Hong Kong affairs and China's internal affairs in any form. Global Times
